title: Towards Quantum Networks: Characterizing Raman Noise over Metropolitan-scale Fiber Network
authors: Marcello Caleffi, Laura d'Avossa, Italo Ignacio Machuca Flores, Marco Grillo, Elena Montella, Angela Sara Cacciapuoti
abstract: The coexistence of quantum and classical signals in optical fiber infrastructures represents a major challenge for large-scale quantum networks, as noise sources such as Raman scattering can significantly impact entanglement distribution, and the quantum protocols based on it. In this work, we analyze Raman scattering in the C-band, used for entanglement distribution, generated by a classical the O-band signal. The main contribution of this study lays in investigating these effects in a real metropolitan-fiber network, moving beyond controlled laboratory experiments to deployed telecommunication environments. Measurements are performed over a 7 km metropolitan fiber link using commercial sources and narrowband lasers. The experimental results shows good agreement between the measurements taken under laboratory conditions, although, within the metropolitan-scale loop, localized spectral anomalies are observed in the deployed fibers. Therefore, our results show that, whenever a quantum signal propagates in the C-band alongside an O-band classical channel within the same fiber, careful selection of the operating frequency is required, as Raman scattering and other real-world noise sources can significantly affect the quality and stability of the quantum transmission. In particular, we identify spectral regions that are less affected by Raman noise, thereby providing practical guidelines for optimal quantum channel allocation. We demonstrate that Raman-induced noise constitutes a dominant contribution to the quantum signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in realistic deployments, beyond background and detector noise. Overall, our findings offer practical insights for deploying quantum communication systems over existing fiber networks, supporting the development of robust and scalable quantum infrastructures.
summary: This paper experimentally characterizes Raman noise generated when classical signals co-propagate with quantum signals in metropolitan optical fiber links. By measuring this noise over a 7 km urban loop, the authors demonstrate that Raman scattering significantly degrades the quantum SNR. The findings offer vital, practical guidelines for allocating optimal frequency channels to enable scalable quantum communication over existing telecom infrastructure.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is how noise, specifically Raman scattering generated by classical O-band signals, degrades quantum entanglement distribution in large-scale metropolitan optical fiber networks.
main_result: Raman-induced noise was found to be a dominant source limiting the quantum signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in realistic deployments. The study provides practical guidelines for selecting optimal C-band spectral regions less susceptible to this noise.
method: The authors conducted measurements over a 7 km metropolitan fiber loop, comparing results from controlled laboratory settings against real-world deployed telecommunication environments using SNSPD detectors.
model_or_system: The system is a standard single-core optical fiber operating in the C-band for quantum signals and co-propagating with classical O-band traffic. The analysis focuses on the physical interaction causing Raman scattering noise within this existing infrastructure.
key_observables: Raman noise contribution to the quantum signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), spectral variations of Raman noise across DWDM channels, and localized spectral anomalies.
important_parameters: Metropolitan fiber link length (7 km), operating bands (O-band classical source vs. C-band quantum detection), and specific frequency windows for channel allocation.
main_assumptions: The study assumes that the co-propagation of signals in the same single-core fiber is the relevant physical scenario, moving beyond idealized laboratory setups to account for environmental inhomogeneities.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the 7 km urban fiber loop setup and the experimental apparatus. Spectra (Fig. 3) compare raw and normalized Raman scattering measurements taken over different path lengths, comparing lab vs. urban data.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of noise in hybrid quantum/classical networks, details the metropolitan-scale experimental setup and methodology for measuring Raman noise, presents comparative spectral results showing consistency but also localized anomalies, and concludes with practical guidelines for channel allocation.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering feasibility of scaling quantum communication by quantifying a dominant real-world noise source (Raman scattering) in existing infrastructure, which is crucial knowledge for developing robust quantum networks.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Scheme of the 7Km urban fiber loop of University of Naples Federico II. The first path, P1, connects Monte Sant’Angelo (MSA) campus to the Engineering Faculty (EF) campus. The loop is closed through the second path, P2, which enables the return transmission of photons back to MSA campus. a) MSA campus hosts the laboratory (Lab), where photons are generated and detected after completing the loop. The campus also contains the Point of Presence (PoP), which provides access to the metropolitan fiber network. b) At the Engineering Faculty (EF) campus, the branches P1 and P2 are interconnected through a patch fiber, thereby establishing the return path toward MSA campus.

Fig. 2: Experimental setup within the National Quantu- mInternet.it testbed. A classical signal in the O-band, gener- ated either by a commercial SFP transmitter or by a narrow- linewidth laser source, is filtered through cascaded WDM modules and launched into the 7Km urban fiber loop. Raman- scattered photons generated in the C-band are spectrally se- lected using a tunable narrowband filter and detected by a superconducting nanowire single-photon detector (SNSPD).

Fig. 3: Experimental results of Raman scattering spectra. C-band SpRS photons generated from O-band classical sources are measured in terms of photon counts per second as a function of wavelength, corresponding to the ITU DWDM channels. The data include measurements obtained using both a narrowband laser source and a commercial SFP transmitter over the full fiber loop (7 km) and a one-way path (3.5 km). In (a) - Raw data, an additional reference measurement with no launched signal is included to identify background contributions.
